correspondence.finding: The southwestern beginning rises north through the Doumic–Moncouche–Le Marié lake-country setting, then follows the north-going aux Sables corridor toward Itomamo. The MRNF southern sheet distinguishes these lakes and the connected hydrographic approach from the nearby Poulin-De Courval, Jalobert and Rouvray settings. No exact name is assigned to the earliest small feeder or every short interlake connection.

The selected line passes through the Itomamo setting and continues north by the Rivière aux Sables approach into Pipmuacan. BAPE Figure 2 explicitly maps the aux Sables watercourse on both sides of Itomamo and distinguishes its northern reservoir route from the eastern Portneuf outlet. Figure 4 and the MRNF sheet show the corresponding reservoir approach. The selected path does not turn down the separate Portneuf river.

The modeled northward continuation and broad eastward turn belong to the western Pipmuacan reservoir corridor. The line then bends through the reservoir toward its eastern outlet region. The MRNF southern sheet and BAPE maps distinguish reservoir water from the entering rivers. This is a generalized reservoir traversal, not evidence that all of it is a natural river reach or that its exact centerline follows present shorelines.

Beyond the Pipmuacan crossing, the selected southeastward route follows the mapped Betsiamites corridor through the Bersimis development setting and downstream toward the Saint-Laurent. BAPE Figure 4 identifies Rivière Betsiamites and separately marks the Pipmuacan and Bersimis 2 impoundments, Lac-Cassé/Desroches works and power developments. CEHQ regional cartography independently distinguishes the Betsiamites descent from the neighboring Portneuf, Sault aux Cochons, Outardes and Manicouagan corridors. The model does not resolve dam, gallery, bypass and tailrace choices.

The long northern selection approaches the Manouanis lake corridor from the northeast, continues south along the mapped upper Betsiamites past the des Prairies/du Bouchon lake setting, and enters Pipmuacan from the north before joining the modeled mainstem in reservoir water. The northern and southern MRNF sheets together show this route, with Rivière Betsiamites explicitly labeled; the CEHQ Region 08 eastern edge and BAPE basin map corroborate the broader corridor. It is selected as a tributary in this object, despite carrying the Betsiamites name upstream. Its earliest short feeder name and exact lake entry/exit points are not assigned.

The final selected reach is the lower Betsiamites/estuarine approach to the Saint-Laurent west of the settlement labeled Betsiamites in the historical BAPE map. The sources establish the drainage and coastal setting, not the selected endpoint as an exact mouth, surveyed tidal limit or full estuarine extent.

The northeastern modeled beginning follows the northward Río Tatamá corridor past the Pueblo Rico setting and joins the San Juan in the Santa Cecilia setting. Readable PNN river labels and the older IGAC map distinguish Tatamá from the San Juan / San Juan Bravo approaching from the northeast. The model has chosen a tributary route for this upper mainstem portion; its beginning is not asserted to be the official river source.

From the Santa Cecilia–Guarato region the selected trunk proceeds generally west through the upper San Juan corridor toward Tadó, then southwest past the Istmina–Andagoya region and down the San Juan valley. The detailed upper sheet, IGAC regional map, CODECHOCÓ San Juan zone and WFP drainage network agree on this receiving-river connection. Adjacent Atrato and Baudó drainage remains separate.

The northern long eastern tributary begins south of the Tatamá massif in the San José del Palmar/Ingará setting, then proceeds west into the broader Tamaná receiving corridor before reaching San Juan. PNN cartography supports the eastern feeder and Ingará alignment; the IGAC maps distinguish Ingará, Surama and Tamaná along the regional connection. No single one of those names is extended over the whole two-piece path, and the precise name of the initial minor feeder and exact downstream name transitions are left unassigned.

The short eastern approach immediately upstream of the large Sipí-side junction lies in the Cajón tributary setting. Regional drainage and CODECHOCÓ zoning support its San Juan connection. The short upper feeder is not independently assigned a hydronym and Cajón is retained as tributary-system context only.

The large eastern branch descends southwest from the cordillera, turns northwest and then west into San Juan in the Sipí–Garrapatas regional corridor. CODECHOCÓ explicitly places Río Garrapatas in the Sipí subzone; the readable regional drainage network supports the selected long loop and its receiving junction. Sipí and Garrapatas are separate component names, not aliases of San Juan, and the exact name transition along the modeled path is not pinned.

Farther downstream, the two long eastern tributary paths have distinct northwestern lower approaches and eastern/southeastern headward legs. Their shapes and connections match the regional drainage layout within CODECHOCÓ’s Copoma/Capoma and other-direct-to-San-Juan subzone, which separately includes Cucurrupí. The municipal diagnosis likewise distinguishes Copomá and Cucurrupí as tributaries. The regional map is sufficient for their San Juan-system membership; exact whole-path individual names are deliberately not assigned from basin labels or the WFP label placement.

The isolated short eastern feeder downstream of those larger tributary junctions lies in the lower San Juan/Munguidó regional setting. Its modeled connection is consistent with the regional basin coverage, but the available scale does not independently name or fully depict this small feeder. Its name remains unknown; Munguidó is not transferred to it solely from proximity.

The southern long tributary runs west through the Calima valley and turns northwest into lower San Juan upstream of the delta. Its broad valley shape, southern position and receiving junction agree with the readable Río Calima drainage line and the independently described Calima–San Juan relationship. Exact headwater initiation, reservoir shoreline and every local bend are outside this regional correspondence.

Below the Calima junction, the selected trunk turns west through the Malaguita/Palestina setting and follows the southern delta continuation toward Boca San Juan near El Choncho. The municipal text distinguishes the northern Cabeceras branch through Docordó from the southern continuation. Official geographical prose explicitly calls that southern watercourse Brazo San Juan and its outlet Boca San Juan. The selected route is therefore not assigned to Togoromá, Charambirá, Chavica or the northern Docordó branch. The endpoint is a generalized coastal approach, not an exact modern mouth or shoreline.

The southwestern model start lies on a short northward feeder south of Kigalik River. The official Lookout Ridge sheet depicts this feeder and the adjoining Kigalik valley near the Kigal high-ground setting without assigning an individual stream name to the feeder. The model then turns east along the Kigalik corridor. Neither the short feeder nor the selected starting point is treated as the officially named source of Kigalik or Ikpikpuk.

The eastward southern reach follows the lower Kigalik River toward the Maybe Creek junction, then turns north into the Ikpikpuk River. The retained BLM report explicitly identifies the confluence of Kigalik River and Maybe Creek as the formation of Ikpikpuk. The eastern Maybe Creek branch and its September Creek setting are not selected headwaters.

The long middle northward section corresponds to the Ikpikpuk River corridor, passing the Howard Hill setting and continuing through its meandering coastal-plain reach. The BLM map separates western approaches including Titaluk/Oumalik and eastern approaches including Price River from that main corridor. These tributaries help identify the selected river but are not separate selected fragments and are not aliases for Ikpikpuk.

The selection departs eastward from the Ikpikpuk corridor before following its lower delta to Smith Bay. The generalized eastward connector traverses the southwestern Teshekpuk lake-plain setting. On the BLM map this modeled departure lies south of the conspicuous western lake/river connection. The map labels Miguakiak River in the western/southern Teshekpuk setting, but that label is not assigned to the complete modeled connector merely because the route links the same broad river and lake areas. No continuous named natural channel is established along that model segment.

The nearly straight eastward crossing runs through Teshekpuk Lake and continues into the eastern lake-margin setting. Teshekpuk remains a separately named lake, not an Ikpikpuk reach or river alias. The modeled cross-lake line and the link into the northeastern lake chain are not identified as surveyed channels, navigable routes, or evidence of eastward drainage from Teshekpuk.

The final northward section corresponds at regional scale to the Garry Creek and elongated-lake corridor east/northeast of Teshekpuk, toward Pogik Bay. The map distinctly shows Smith River farther west and Kogru River farther east/south. The selected terminal point remains within the inland lake-rich corridor, short of the mapped coast. Garry Creek is supported as a component corridor name; the model does not establish that every traversed lake or intervening generalized connector bears that hydronym.

The southeastern beginning runs north on the western Buriti drainage side before turning west through the eastern Preto corridor north of the Chapadinha/Anapurus setting. The CPRM basin map and ANA network map show that connected approach separately from the more southerly Munim trunk. The 2011 report explicitly distinguishes the Preto headwater region in Buriti and its Anapurus–Mata Roma–Chapadinha boundary corridor. The exact first modeled vertex is not claimed to be the reported spring or an official river source.

After its long westward eastern reach, the selected course turns north, then west through the São Benedito do Rio Preto setting and bends south toward the receiving Munim junction near the Nina Rodrigues corridor. This distinctive detour is visible in the acquired basin map and the retained ANA sheet. The SEMA table places the São Benedito station on Rio Preto at that middle selected reach, corroborating the component name rather than inferring it solely from a town name.

The mainstem-role fragment boundary lies near the Preto-to-Munim connection. The subsequent selection turns northwest and north through the lower Munim corridor. The southern Munim approach and the Iguará river near Vargem Grande are mapped as distinct contributing routes, not selected replacement headwaters. The station table separately assigns its Vargem Grande-area records to Munim and Iguará, which prevents treating all these neighboring channels as one uniformly named reach.

The lower course continues north past the Presidente Juscelino, Cachoeira Grande and Morros settings toward Axixá, while the eastern Buriti and other side drainages remain separate. The full northward route is shown by both regional maps. Colored geological/alluvial units around the channel on the CPRM sheet are not interpreted as lake polygons or reservoir passages.

The selected endpoint is on the lower Munim beyond the Axixá vicinity, approaching the São José bay setting. The source maps and report distinguish that receiving bay from the river and from the western Itapecuru/Arraial coastal system. The model is not extended through the complete bay or to an offshore Atlantic endpoint, and no precise present-day tidal or shoreline boundary is assigned.

scope_limit: MAIN_RIV groups and model mainstem roles do not establish a uniform name for every included reach, tributary or lake passage. Source observations support only the stated representative identity or hold.
publication_boundary: Own factual observations, attribution and official public URLs only; source originals, images, complete coordinates and private evidence remain omitted.
